thesis: Same horizon as round 1, same mechanism: a multi-quarter EMA(100)/EMA(300) cross only fires once a trend has persisted long enough to move an average with a multi-hundred-session memory, so it structurally cannot chase noise -- the cost is entering and exiting later than any faster system, which is why a01-trend's round-2 book (a 20/50-EMA cross on an overlapping set of these same cross-asset names) is not a competitor to this card, it is the fast half of the same natural experiment on similar instruments. What round 2 actually changes for this discipline is not the rule, it is what round 1's fixed universe could not supply: independent regime turns. Round 1's 12-name universe was one AI-capex cycle in twelve wrappers; I measured its own EMA(50)/EMA(200) uptrend runs at median 186.5 / mean 239 sessions, with pullbacks up to p90=18.0%, and set a 22% stop on that basis. This round I chose the opposite of that -- deliberately away from equities -- and measured, not assumed, what the round-2 brief's correlation table implied: on 259-session trailing returns through 2026-02-13, treasuries and precious metals are genuinely decoupled from equity beta (TLT vs SPY corr +0.090, GDX vs SPY +0.210) while international equities are not (EWZ +0.491, FXI +0.522, INDA +0.477 vs SPY -- confirmed, matching the brief's warning that 'uncorrelated emerging markets' is not supported here). My final seven-symbol book -- TLT, GDX, DBC, EWZ, FXI, INDA, CPER -- has a measured mean pairwise correlation of 0.23 across all 21 pairs (full matrix computed, range -0.12 to +0.46), versus 0.589 for round 1's semiconductor cluster and 0.581 for the round-2 brief's own US-sector-ETF measurement. That is the actual lever this round gives a slow-trend discipline: not more trades, but trades that do not share one cause. I explicitly tested the brief's prompt that 'long bond and gold trends are famously long-lived' rather than taking it as given, and it only half holds in this data. Bonds: yes -- TLT's EMA(50)/EMA(200) uptrend runs measured median 187.0 / mean 206.6 sessions, comparable to or longer than round 1's semis regime, with tame pullbacks (p90 16.8%, p95 20.5%). Gold: no, or at least not through the only proxy this roster offers -- GLD itself is not in the round-2 list, so gold exposure here is GDX (miners), and mining equities carry operating leverage the metal does not: GDX's uptrend runs measured median 148.0 / mean 168.6 sessions, shorter than TLT's and shorter than round 1's semis, with a 42.2% annualised volatility (measured, trailing 259 sessions) that is closer to a semiconductor stock than to the 'calm ballast' gold's reputation implies -- consistent with the round-2 brief's own note that GLD's measured 24.9% vol already undercuts that reputation before you add mining-equity leverage on top. Mechanism and counterparty are unchanged from round 1: slow, multi-quarter capital reallocation (rate-cycle positioning in bonds, real-asset/EM growth flows in commodities and emerging equities) that a filter with a multi-hundred-session memory can catch, working against momentum and mean-reversion traders who exit on the pullbacks this system is sized to sit through. I did not rescale the stop per symbol because the engine cannot: measured 259-session annualised volatility across this book ranges 11.9% (TLT) to 42.2% (GDX), a 3.5x spread, and measured EMA(50)/EMA(200) pullback p90s range from 8.0% (DBC) to 24.8% (CPER). I set the single stop_loss_pct at 0.25 -- just above CPER's p90 (24.8%), the tightest fit in the book -- which means it is a real, biteable risk control on GDX/CPER/EWZ/FXI but functionally slack on TLT/DBC/INDA (whose own p90s are 16.8%/8.0%/10.9%); I am stating that mismatch rather than pretending one number fits a 12%-vol bond ETF and a 42%-vol miner ETF equally. On expected trade count: each symbol's own full-history EMA(100)/EMA(300) up-cross frequency (once every roughly 130-590 sessions per name, all measured, not assumed) implies about 1-3 fresh entries across this seven-symbol book over the 127-session trading window -- the same order of magnitude as round 1's 2-4, not a multiple of it, and still very likely under the ten-trade threshold this tournament needs for a p-value. Cross-asset breadth does not fix that; a slow filter fires rarely regardless of what it is pointed at. What it changes is that if those 1-3 trades do land, they are not all restatements of one AI-capex bet: as of the design cutoff, TLT is the one name in this book *not* currently in an EMA(100)/EMA(300) uptrend (last cross was a down-cross, 1247 sessions ago) while GDX, DBC, EWZ, FXI, INDA and CPER all are, with time-since-last-cross ranging from 73 sessions (DBC, the freshest) to 492 (CPER, the most dormant) -- meaning a fresh signal, if one comes, is unlikely to be simultaneous across names. I am not adding instruments to chase a trade count I already know this rule cannot deliver; the honest case for this round-2 universe is diversification of cause, not volume of trades.
